papers.title: RoDPAA: A Robust Dissimilarity-Based Principal Angle Analysis Framework for Multi-View Microbiome Data Integration
papers.abstract: Multiview microbiome studies profile the same participants across body sites or molecular layers, but integration is hampered by sparse, compositional data, modest sample sizes and methods that recognize only exact sharing. We present RoDPAA (Robust Dissimilarity-based Principal Angle Analysis), a framework that represents each view through any data-appropriate dissimilarity, such as Bray--Curtis, without log-ratio transformation or likelihood assumptions. RoDPAA aligns view-specific signal subspaces through principal angles, captures complete and partial sharing, and tests by permutation how many components are shared, using only eigendecomposition and little tuning. In Gaussian simulations, RoDPAA matched JIVE and MOFA given true ranks, ran faster and alone recovered the shared dimension in every replicate. In two inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) cohorts with sparse, zero-inflated data, Bray--Curtis-based RoDPAA recovered shared structure that was stable to prevalence filtering, whereas log-ratio-based alternatives were not. Its leading microbiome--metabolome factors, learned without disease labels, were the only ones associated with IBD.

papers.title: Somatic Structural Variant Discovery from Tumor Specific Strings Computed Against a Draft Composite Germline Reference
papers.abstract: Somatic structural variants (SVs) are among the most clinically relevant genomic alterations in cancer. However, their accurate detection remains challenging due to complex genomic rearrangements, repetitive genomic regions, difficulties in distinguishing somatic variants from germline variation and sequencing artifacts, and limited sequencing support for low-frequency events. Existing mapping-based somatic SV callers are susceptible to alignment ambiguities in repetitive regions and near complex SV breakpoints, while approaches relying on comparisons of independently generated tumor and normal variant callsets may propagate errors from both callsets. Building on the concept of specific strings, previously applied to germline SV discovery, we introduce VESPA-SS, a novel approach for detecting somatic SVs from paired tumor-normal long-read whole-genome sequencing data. VESPA-SS directly extracts somatic SV signals using specific strings computed from tumor reads against a Draft Composite Germline Reference, without requiring initial read mapping or a high-quality germline assembly. These signals are subsequently clustered and refined through consensus sequence generation and alignment-based procedures to identify somatic SVs. Evaluation on real PacBio HiFi datasets demonstrates that VESPA-SS outperforms state-of-the-art somatic SV callers, achieving F1 scores exceeding 0.92 and 0.90 on the well-characterized HG008 and COLO829 cancer cell lines, respectively, compared with the highest F1 scores of 0.86 and 0.85 achieved by the evaluated methods. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of specific string based signal extraction for accurate somatic SV discovery and establish a new computational paradigm for identifying complex genomic alterations in cancer. VESPA-SS is freely available at https://github.com/dcmonti/VESPA.

papers.title: LeadWeaver: Topology-Aware Masked-Lead Modeling for Robust 12-Lead ECG Diagnosis
papers.abstract: Clinical electrocardiography is organized as a structured set of correlated leads, yet most neural ECG classifiers assume that all twelve leads are present, correctly ordered, and acquired under the same device conditions at training and deployment. We propose LeadWeaver, a topology-aware ECG representation model designed for diagnosis under missing, corrupted, or device-shifted leads. LeadWeaver represents each lead as a temporal token stream, couples leads through a fixed-plus-learned physiological lead graph, and performs masked-lead latent completion rather than waveform synthesis. A reliability router estimates which observed leads should dominate each diagnostic decision, while a consistency objective aligns complete-lead and incomplete-lead predictions. We evaluate the model on PTB-XL and CPSC-style settings using complete-input diagnosis, arbitrary missing-lead subsets, lead corruption, cross-dataset transfer, calibration, and selective prediction. The central hypothesis is that robust ECG diagnosis requires explicitly modeling both inter-lead topology and uncertainty about unavailable evidence, rather than treating missing channels as zero-valued inputs.

papers.title: MOCHI enables systematic identification of candidate independent intronic transcriptional signals from short-read RNA-seq data
papers.abstract: Standard short-read RNA-seq analysis pipelines quantify expression over annotated exons and disregard signals mapped to introns, thereby missing independently transcribed intronic RNAs. Existing strategies depend on annotation, biologically crude whole-intron quantification, or subjective, low-throughput manual genome-browser inspection. We present MOCHI (Mapping of Cryptic Hidden Intronic Transcripts), a framework that couples reference-independent, k-mer-based signal discovery with reference-guided genomic interpretation and a custom multi-step filtering module to systematically curate potential independent intronic transcription units from strand-specific short-read RNA-seq data. On two simulated datasets, MOCHI recovered annotated sense-intronic long non-coding RNAs removed from the reference and distinguished them from intronic signal confounders. Across paired ribosomal RNA-depleted and poly(A)-selected libraries from ten cancer cell lines, MOCHI curated candidates whose host introns are strongly enriched for a transcription-initiation signal. Candidate expression is largely uncoupled from host-gene exons, and their genomic features resemble those of annotated long non-coding RNAs. In ten matched cohorts from The Cancer Genome Atlas, candidates were detected in tumor samples, and a subset was associated with overall survival after adjustment for age and host-gene expression. Consequently, MOCHI extends the transcriptomic landscape that can be mined from existing short-read RNA-seq data and provides a curated resource of candidate intronic transcripts for downstream analyses.

papers.title: Toward space-optimal approximate colored indexes at scale
papers.abstract: Searching current petabase-scale sequence repositories requires indexes that combine compact storage with high query throughput. Although exact colored indexes retain complete sequence information, their construction and storage costs can become substantial for highly diverse collections. Indexes based on approximate membership query (AMQ) filters offer a compact alternative with fast construction and queries. Being hash-based, these indexes support different seeding schemes without structural changes, while sampling can reduce storage requirements, construction time and query time by an order of magnitude. Within the AMQ framework, querying many independent filters causes scattered memory accesses, reducing throughput. This motivates interleaved filters, which address this weakness by storing filter slots contiguously by position, enabling cache-friendly access and simultaneous membership queries. However, existing implementations face a trade-off between guaranteed construction and space-efficiency. Here, we introduce a new indexing framework based on interleaved ZOR filters, fingerprint-based structures with guaranteed construction that require only approximately 1% more space than the theoretical minimum for AMQ. To exploit redundancy between genomes, we introduce a color-preserving merging mechanism that extends fingerprints with membership bits, allowing multiple genomes to share a filter while retaining their individual identities. Together with a lightweight, sketch-based layout planner, this mechanism yields a compact index structure that accommodates collections with widely varying genome sizes and degrees of similarity. Our third contribution extends the AMQ framework beyond contiguous -mers through a low-density minimizer scheme alongside efficient implementations of sensitive seeds, including gapped -mers and randstrobes. We implement these methods in Zindex, a parallel, SIMD-accelerated Rust index that scales to millions of genomes while supporting diverse seeding and sampling schemes. Zindex indexes the latest RefSeq release of 564,401 assembled genomes in under 22 hours, producing a 289.5 GB index. It further scales to all 2,763,297 genomes of AllTheBacteria, producing a 406.3 GB index in four days with a peak memory footprint of 43.8 GB. Availability. Zindex is available at https://github.com/Malfoy/Zindex

papers.title: scCircaSim: A Circadian Simulator for Single-Cell and Spatial Transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Motivation: Simulated single-cell and spatial transcriptomic datasets that capture circadian dynamics while providing known ground truth remain scarce, limiting systematic evaluation of circadian analysis methods. Results: We developed scCircaSim to generate circadian single-cell and spatial transcriptomic data from a single-time-point reference. The framework combines phase progression with reference-derived network propagation of anchor gene rhythms and incorporates neighborhood effects for spatial simulation. Outputs retain reference heterogeneity and provide known cell or spot phases, rhythmicity labels, and gene-level mesor, amplitude, and phase values. Validation showed retention of reference structure and recovery of specified temporal patterns. Benchmarks of four cell phase inference methods and three rhythmic gene analysis methods revealed differences in phase accuracy, rhythmicity detection, and parameter recovery. scCircaSim supports reproducible method evaluation and preliminary experimental planning. Availability and Implementation: scCircaSim is implemented in R and available at https://github.com/Liwei-DynamicsLab/scCircaSim.

papers.title: Hierarchical Temporal Transformer for Cancer Grade Prediction and Cross-Cancer Transfer Learning from Pathology Reports
papers.abstract: Background: Language models for cancer reports usually read one document at a time and are tested on tumour types seen in training. Continuous-time sequence models address the first gap, but whether they use visit timing, not just order, is seldom tested. Methods: We developed the Hierarchical Temporal Transformer (HTT), which encodes reports with adapted BiomedBERT and reads the sequence with a cancer-type-conditioned temporal transformer. We evaluated it against best-possible AUROC ceilings on two synthetic benchmarks, one with the label stated in the text and one recoverable only from tumour sizes and visit intervals (ten seeds). Diagnostics led to an interval-aware time code (HTT-IA). On 4,786 TCGA pathology reports in 14 types, three types were withheld, and a text-only HTT was compared with a survival model. Results: On the phrase benchmark HTT reached AUROC 0.931 +/- 0.012 against 0.913 +/- 0.007 for a last-report baseline (+0.018, 95% CI -0.009 to +0.050); dates cannot raise the ceiling there. On the growth benchmark the initial time code scored 0.790, equal to a no-time model (0.787), whereas HTT-IA reached 0.843 (+0.053, 0.026 to 0.082) against ceilings of 0.894 without and 0.979 with dates. On unseen tumour types HTT reached 0.925 +/- 0.007, equal to in-distribution performance and to a single-report baseline. Text-only macro C-index was 0.592 (CALM 0.626-0.652). Conclusion: Cross-type transfer is carried by the pre-trained encoder. Visit timing is used only when the data make it identifiable and the time code is on a clinical scale. Ceilings, order-only ablations and re-dating probes are inexpensive checks for such models.

papers.title: Deducing splicing events from transcript sets with splicelogic
papers.abstract: Long-read RNA sequencing captures a greater proportion of full-length transcripts, enabling more accurate isoform identification, discovery of novel isoforms, and more precise differential transcript usage analysis. However, comparing transcripts, whether between conditions or between sets such as novel and annotated isoforms, yields complex isoform changes that are hard to manipulate, summarize, and visualize. This is compounded by vertical integration of some tools, where downstream analysis depends on the specific output of a particular upstream tool. To address this gap, we have developed splicelogic, an R/Bioconductor package that makes transcript-set comparisons biologically interpretable by turning them into discrete splicing events, such as exon skipping, alternative splice sites, intron retention, and alternative transcription start and end sites. We designed splicelogic to integrate easily with existing RNA-seq workflows and tools. The splicelogic functions are modular, readable, and extensible, making it easy for users to adapt core logic to their own custom scientific questions or novel splicing definitions. By obtaining interpretable splicing events from transcript changes, splicelogic enables downstream analyses, including annotation of RNA-binding protein recognition sites, alongside summary statistics and visualization. The splicelogic package is publicly available and distributed through Bioconductor.

papers.title: Joint protein-DNA language modeling enables prediction and engineering of DNA recognition specificity
papers.abstract: Protein-DNA recognition specificity underlies transcriptional regulation, DNA replication, chromatin remodeling and genome editing. Protein-DNA recognition depends on both interacting sequences, yet language models that learn this cross-molecular dependence explicitly during pretraining remain limited. Here, we developed the Protein-DNA Language Models (PDLMs), interaction-aware language models that jointly represent protein and DNA sequences. PDLMs were built by continued pretraining from ESM2 with masked language modeling on paired protein-DNA sequences. A shared encoder places amino acids and nucleotides in the same molecular context, enabling conditional sequence scoring and transferable pair representations. We further introduced a domain-aware masking strategy that increased masking probability within DNA-binding domains to strengthen learning of interaction-relevant regions. Across downstream tasks, PDLMs improved protein-DNA pair classification relative to independent-encoder baselines and supported prediction of mutation-associated binding changes. Zero-shot scoring recovered known changes in DNA-recognition specificity and prioritized variants with higher editing activity. Learned representations also supported cross-study prediction of base editor activity. After fine-tuning on transcription factor binding data, PDLMs predicted DNA motifs directly from protein sequences. Together, PDLMs provide a framework for interaction-aware biomolecular language modeling, with potential applications in protein engineering and genome editing.

papers.title: Development of a Pan-Proteome Multi-Epitope Vaccine Candidate Against Nipah Virus Using Reverse Vaccinology and Immunoinformatics Approaches
papers.abstract: Nipah virus (NiV) is a high-consequence zoonotic pathogen for which no licensed human vaccine is currently available. This study applied a consensus-guided pan-proteome immunoinformatics framework to design and prioritize a multi-epitope vaccine candidate using sequence information from all nine NiV proteins. A total of 901 NiV protein sequences were retrieved, of which 842 passed quality filtering and were processed through clustering, multiple-sequence alignment, and protein-specific consensus generation. Consensus-derived fragments were screened for cytotoxic T-lymphocyte, helper T-lymphocyte, and B-cell epitopes, followed by multi-criterion filtering based on antigenicity, allergenicity, toxicity, conservancy, class-specific immune-response properties, and human-proteome similarity. Ten epitope-selection strategies were combined with two adjuvant candidates and three construct architectures to generate 60 vaccine constructs. Shortlisted candidates were subsequently evaluated for physicochemical properties, HLA population coverage, structural characteristics, conformational B-cell epitopes, TLR3 docking, molecular dynamics, immune-response simulation, and expression-oriented optimization. VC033_V6_BD_L03 construct was prioritized as the lead candidate and showed combined predicted population coverage of 99.78% worldwide and 99.96% in South Asia. Docking against human TLR3 structure 1ZIW yielded a ClusPro score of -1624.8. During a 100-ns molecular-dynamics simulation, the complex underwent early conformational reorganization followed by lower late-phase structural variation and persistent interchain hydrogen bonding. MM/GBSA analysis yielded a mean interaction-energy estimate of -20.52, 15.42 kcal/mol. C-ImmSim predicted coordinated humoral and cellular responses, while codon optimization generated a 1,539-bp expression sequence compatible with virtual cloning into pET-28a(+). These analyses prioritize VC033_V6_BD_L03 as a consensus-derived, pan-proteome NiV multi-epitope vaccine candidate for experimental evaluation of expression, immunogenicity, safety, and protective efficacy.

papers.title: Bioprocess Modeling Made Easy With Hybrax
papers.abstract: Hybrid models that embed neural networks in ordinary differential equations are increasingly popular in bioprocess modeling, but they are challenging to set up. Much of the effort goes into the code around the model: wet-lab data must be imported and pre-processed, feeds and sampling must be accounted for in the balance equations, and a training loop with cross-validation must be set up. Researchers usually write this code from scratch for each project. In addition, no widely adopted format for bioprocess data exists, and datasets are mostly published in bespoke spreadsheets or not at all. As a result, models and datasets from the literature are difficult to reproduce, reuse, or compare.We present Hybrax, an open-source Python framework that addresses these problems. It combines a flexible format for bioprocess data with a customizable end-to-end training pipeline for mechanistic and hybrid models. Hybrax derives the transport terms in the process dynamics automatically and provides the utilities needed for training, so that researchers can focus on developing the model itself. It also facilitates model sharing and reproducibility: each training checkpoint contains the model parameters, code, configuration, and training data required to run the model or retrain it from scratch. We demonstrate Hybrax by re-implementing two models from the literature, one trained on real-world E. coli data and one on synthetic HEK293 data, with performance comparable to the original models. Hybrax is available at https://github.com/hybrax/hybrax.

papers.title: Generative 3D Spatial Reconstruction of Cellular Organization from Single Cell Expression
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing profiles cellular states at scale but removes their three-dimensional (3D) spatial organization. Reconstructing this organization requires recovering not only individual cell positions but also the physical size, geometry, and neighborhoods of an entire tissue. Existing methods either map cells onto measured spatial references or reconstruct two-dimensional sections independently, leaving the joint reconstruction of a new 3D specimen unresolved. Moreover, predicting the average plausible position of each cell can reduce per-cell error while compressing tissue geometry. We introduce ORBIS, a generative framework that jointly reconstructs whole 3D specimens from single-cell gene expression without requiring a spatial reference at inference. ORBIS learns spatial organization through flow matching in a shared physical coordinate frame, using training views sampled from sparse serial sections, tissue blocks, and whole specimens. At inference, a shared spatial state is iteratively updated through dynamically regrouped windows, enabling the generation of millions of cell positions without independently reconstructing and stitching tissue regions. We evaluate physical size, cell-population shape, per-cell placement, and neighborhood organization separately to distinguish accurate tissue geometry from low per-cell error. Across eight held-out specimens spanning whole mouse brains, thick brain blocks, and Drosophila embryos, ORBIS achieves lower cell-population shape error than all five evaluated baselines on every test and reconstructs specimens containing up to 3.7 million cells. On a single GPU, ORBIS samples million-cell brains in 0.9-2.8 minutes, approximately 38 times faster than the sampler of LUNA-3D, our 3D extension of the state-of-the-art generative spatial reconstruction method LUNA. On two held-out brain tests, sampling reduces size error by 3.3-fold and shape error by 1.8-fold compared with a single-call variant. On an independent dissociated single-cell brain atlas, ORBIS returns on average 37.9% of each region's cells to their dissection region across 23 regions, compared with 28.5% for LUNA-3D.

papers.title: pLM-bVAE: protein language model-enhanced binary representation improves quantum annealing-based protein sequence design
papers.abstract: Quantum annealing (QA) has been explored as an approach for protein design in vast combinatorial sequence spaces. Applying QA to protein sequence design requires amino acid sequences to be encoded as binary vectors, and optimized vectors to be decoded back into amino acid sequences. Thus, both the quality of binary encoding and sequence reconstruction accuracy are important for effective QA-based optimization. Binary variational autoencoder (bVAE) has been used to map protein sequences to binary representations in QA-based protein sequence design. However, bVAE was originally developed for natural language modeling, and its suitability for proteins has not been systematically evaluated. Here, we present pLM-bVAE, which incorporates protein representations derived from a pretrained protein language model (pLM) into the original bVAE model. In computational experiments on three public protein variant datasets, pLM-bVAE showed higher sequence reconstruction accuracy and binary encoding performance than bVAE. Moreover, we incorporated pLM-bVAE into a QA-based protein sequence design framework. Across all three datasets, pLM-bVAE generated more high-scoring sequences with greater sequence dissimilarity from the training and validation data than bVAE. Our results demonstrate that pLM-bVAE provides an effective binary representation for improving QA-based protein sequence design. Availability The source code used in this manuscript is available at https://github.com/hueda8/pLM-bVAE.

papers.title: Multimodal cellular context enables molecular phenotyping from single-molecule trajectories
papers.abstract: Single-molecule tracking (SMT) provides direct measurements of molecular dynamics in living cells, but motion alone rarely specifies the underlying biological process, without accounting for the cellular environment in which that motion occurs. Here, we present MIST (Multimodal Interpretation of Single-molecule Trajectories), a framework that brings the paradigm of image-based profiling to single molecules by integrating trajectory dynamics, emitter properties and cellular context into a common, reusable phenotype space. Using a reference panel of nine proteins in live Escherichia coli, we show that multimodal context more than doubled protein-specific information relative to trajectory features alone, a gap that learned trajectory representations did not close. MIST allowed de novo identification of shared transcription-translation phenotype at the nucleoid periphery. A fixed reference space detected effects of previously uncharacterized MukB ATPase mutations without retraining. MIST provides an interpretable and extensible framework for comparing proteins, mutants and conditions within a common space of molecular phenotypes.

papers.title: Label-free flow operators and stability operators from single-cell time courses: what local dynamical operators can and cannot identify
papers.abstract: Local Jacobians of single-cell dynamics are used to locate unstable cells along trajectories, but what they identify from measured data has rarely been tested against independent truth. We present scJDO2, which separates two per-cell operators by the time information they require: a score operator, the Hessian of a score-matched log density, available from any snapshot; and a flow operator, the Jacobian of a drift fitted to a measured velocity, here estimated label-free from a sampled time course by entropic optimal transport. Both are summarized in a shared operator space of magnitude-free descriptors, with the invariance of each stated, and evaluated with pre-registered tests. On synthetic data calibrated to six real datasets, the flow operator from the time course alone separated fate-bifurcation cells from committed cells on held-out seeds (AUC 0.89-1.00) with a-priori settings; tuning on development seeds overfit. On LARRY lineage-traced hematopoiesis, its fitted drift predicted the clonal displacement of barcoded cells beyond population movement (Spearman 0.56, permutation p < 0.001; 0.50 after removing the mean shift) and a held-out sampling day better than mean-displacement and no-movement baselines (energy distance 0.69, 95 % CI 0.66-0.73, vs 0.87 and 0.88); lineage thus validates the velocity, not {lambda}. Mini-batch transport reproduced dense transport (velocity cosine 0.9998) and scaled to all 130,887 cells (transport 5 min and 2.5 GB; drift fit and Jacobians 21 min and 1.3 GB). On an independent simulator it detected two of three bifurcations and two of three cycles and never reported instability on linear trajectories. Several readings failed. Neither operator recovers the values of the true Jacobian; the flow operators leading eigenvalue ranks branching cells empirically. The flow operator depends on the transport metric and inverts on Factor Analysis. Operator archetypes isolated bifurcation cells but did not outperform expression clustering and were unstable across fit seeds. The score operator did not predict CRISPRi knockdown responses or sister-cell fate coherence. A confirmatory test of transition timing could not be constructed, and diffusion is not identifiable at typical sampling intervals. The released software reports these diagnostics.

papers.title: Hub labeling makes exact distance calculation practical for large human pangenome graphs
papers.abstract: Pangenome graphs are now a standard reference representation, and tools built on them depend on fast minimum-distance queries between graph positions, for example, when clustering seed matches during read alignment. The baseline distance index, previously used by the vg toolkit, answers such queries based on a decomposition of the graph into nested subgraphs called "snarls". Within each snarl, the index uses a dense all-pairs distance matrix. Because such a matrix is quadratic in a snarl's number of children, the large, complex snarls that often occur in many pangenome graphs dominate the overall index size. This means whole-genome graphs can be impractical to index. To mitigate this, the baseline distance index does not fully index the largest snarls, and thus cannot itself answer certain queries involving them. We replace the dense matrix with a hub labeling for snarls above a size limit. Because hub labeling and associated methods are defined for directed graphs, we introduce a directed representation of a snarl's bidirected internal "net graph", whose shortest path lengths are the net graph's minimum walk lengths. Hub labels are built using pruned landmark labeling, ordered by a contraction hierarchy. On four human chromosome pangenomes, our hub-labeling-based distance index indexes every snarl in 0.9 GB to 3.0 GB at a snarl limit of 500, an estimated 28x to 119x less space than dense distance matrices would need for those snarls with more than 500 children, and supports the 3-18.6% of node-to-node queries that the previous index cannot answer by itself. On the queries both indexes can answer, query time distributions broadly overlap. We explore the snarl limit parameter space and are able to build indexes under 50 GB for four human whole-genome pangenomes in under 6 hours, where we estimate dense matrices could have required multiple terabytes.

papers.title: Integrative Multiomics Analysis of the Angiogenesis-EMT Interface in Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma
papers.abstract: Angiogenesis and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) are key hallmarks that contribute to the progression of oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), but whether the two programs vary simultaneously across tumors and how much of this reflects tumor composition remain unclear. We scored predefined, non-overlapping 20-gene angiogenesis and EMT signatures with a rank-based method in 342 primary oral cavity tumors from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA-OSCC). The two programs were strongly correlated (Spearman rho = 0.809, P = 2.7 x 10^-80), and 2,396 bridge genes were associated with both programs across the transcriptome. The bridge genes were enriched in pathways associated with focal adhesion and extracellular matrix-receptor interaction. In the cellular case, fibroblast and endothelial marker scores were prominent and correlated with the program scores. The coupling was attenuated but remained positive after joint adjustment for tumor purity and stromal and immune scores (partial rho = 0.406) and with an epithelial-restricted EMT score (rho = 0.710). Further correlation was performed with a partial EMT (pEMT), which shows a significant positive correlation (rho = 0.59) and an inverse correlation with tumor purity (rho = -0.70). 146 final gene candidates were found using multi-omic evidence and candidate-level testing on the external cohort GSE30784; after adjusting for inferred cell fractions, 101 of these candidates supported the dual program. For thorough characterization, three candidates with an emphasis on OSMR, MICAL2, and LHFPL2 were chosen. Additional CPTAC data were used to confirm protein-level support, which was strongest for MICAL2. No significant connection was seen between the Interface score and overall survival (hazard ratio per 1-SD increase, 0.92; 95% CI, 0.78-1.08). These results describe a coordinated angiogenesis-EMT transcriptional state in OSCC that is attenuated but retained after accounting for tumor composition, and nominate candidate genes for experimental study.

papers.title: Generative Models for Novel Enzymatic Reactions: How Far Do They Go?
papers.abstract: Enzyme function prediction is a long-standing problem in biology, and deep learning methods have recently become popular to improve performance on this task. While most of these models focus on classifying enzymes or mapping them to known reactions, predicting unknown biochemical reactions remains underexplored. Here we thoroughly examine an approach that generates reactions absent from the training data from the enzyme alone. Existing methods such as BLASTp or CLIPZyme cannot, by design, output reactions that are absent from their training data or were not supplied at inference. The closest prior model, RxnPred, reports high fingerprint-similarity scores on held-out enzymes, a less stringent criterion than exact recovery, but fails to recover the correct answer on unseen reactions. We present a structure-conditioned generative model that outputs a complete reaction, reactants and products, and evaluate it on EnzymeMap_x, a reaction-disjoint benchmark in which no test reaction appears in training, under exact, stereo-respecting scoring. On this benchmark, within 400 sampled candidates, the model generates the complete, correct reaction for 25.0% of the subset of test enzyme--reaction pairs whose reaction is a new combination of metabolites seen in training. Surprisingly, it also correctly generates a few reactions composed of metabolites it has not seen in training (1.6%), though their embeddings are present in the vocabulary. With a lower budget, re-ranking places the correct reaction first for 5.6% of pairs and in the top ten for 12.4%, when the reaction is assumed not to be already known (0.2% and 8.1% without that assumption) along with confidence scores. Assessed more leniently, the model produces at least one correct reaction known for the enzyme (usually memorised from training) for 71.2% of test pairs. Going further, without any retraining, a sequence-only model given the reactants as well as the enzyme produces the correct product set for 9.5% of pairs within five candidates, without re-ranking. We also present head-to-head comparisons on these tasks with BLASTp, DIAMOND, RxnPred and Horizyn. Structure conditioning improves fingerprint similarity on homology-stratified splits, but a matched sequence-only ablation at the best configuration finds no measurable effect on exact recovery. Data coverage and chemical initialisation of the vocabulary seem to matter more than encoder geometry.

papers.title: spearfish: ultrafast Δ-mapping of long reads to redundant transcriptomes
papers.abstract: In a transcriptome, isoforms share most of their sequence, and gene families add further near-copies. Yet most long-read mappers treat each isoform as a separate target and repeat seeding, chaining and alignment for each. We introduce spearfish, a long-read mapper built for this redundancy. Its delta mapping ({Delta}-mapping) computes each target's alignment-score difference from the best candidate. It skips sequence that all candidates share, which cannot change the difference, and aligns where they differ once per distinct sequence rather than once per target. Seeds come from locally consistent parsing (LCP), so every isoform that contains an exon receives the same seeds in its interior. Collapsing them gives a core graph, a de Bruijn-like graph whose size is bounded by the distinct exonic sequence plus a small term per splice junction, independent of the number of isoforms. Over this graph, spearfish computes the exact colinear chaining score of every candidate transcript, sharing dynamic-programming state among transcripts via a procedure which we prove is equivalent to chaining on each transcript separately. Across RNA-seq experiments, using 32 threads, spearfish maps reads 26-83x faster than minimap2 in at most a seventh of the memory, and 2.6-11.3x faster than lr-kallisto's pseudoalignment. On simulated reads it ranks the true transcript first more often than minimap2 on HiFi reads and within 0.5 percentage points of it on ONT reads at 95% accuracy. When using spearfish's {Delta}-mapping with oarfish for abundance estimation, the abundance estimates match or improve on those that make use of minimap2's alignments on both simulated reads (especially when they are untrimmed) and on seven SG-NEx runs with spike-ins, and quantification is 3.0-8.8x faster than lr-kallisto in going from reads to abundances.

papers.title: TestNet-PA: Sampling-Zero-Aware Inference of Microbial Presence-Absence Networks
papers.abstract: Microbial presence-absence networks, also referred to as co-occurrence networks, characterize patterns of coexistence and incompatibility among taxa. However, sequencing-based presence--absence analysis can be compromised by pervasive 'sampling zeros' in microbiome data, causing widely used methods such as Fisher's exact test to identify spurious co-occurrence dependence. To our knowledge, no existing method is designed to account for sampling zeros in this setting. We introduce TestNet-PA, a method for testing pairwise microbial co-occurrence dependence. TestNet-PA models each observed zero as arising from a mixture of 'structural' and 'sampling' zeros, with the mixing probabilities governed by library size and relative abundance. Because the relative abundance underlying an observed zero is unobserved, we impute it by borrowing information from other samples. We then construct a quasi-likelihood and develop an EM algorithm to infer dependence between the underlying true presence--absence statuses. Extensive simulations based on real gut, vaginal, and oral microbiome data templates showed that TestNet-PA consistently controlled the FDR while maintaining good sensitivity. By contrast, Fisher's exact test generally yielded inflated FDR. Analyses of the three real microbiome datasets further illustrated how accounting for sampling zeros can affect the inferred co-occurrence networks.

papers.title: RadMultiBench: A Reproducible Dual-Task Benchmark Exposing the Limits of Pre-Trained Vision-Language Models Across Thoracic and Breast Imaging
papers.abstract: We present RadMultiBench, a multimodal benchmark of 6,148 medical images paired with expert radiological impressions across five categories--Breast Cancer, Lung Benign, Lung Malignant, Pneumonia, and Tuberculosis--targeting two core clinical tasks: automated report generation and disease classification. To enable reliable, repeatable experimentation, we provide a reproducible pipeline for data ingestion, de-identification, split management, and standardized reporting of text and classification metrics, facilitating dataset versioning and continuous benchmark testing. We compare three architectures: (1) a classical CNN-RNN with Bahdanau attention (ResNet-LSTM), (2) a general-domain vision-language (V-L) prefix-projection model (CLIP-GPT), and (3) a domain-specific V-L prefix-projection model (BioViL-T). Results reveal a sharp performance divide: the ResNet-LSTM attains near-perfect classification (99.5% accuracy) and is the only model to generate coherent reports (BLEU-4 = 0.021), whereas both prefix-projection models catastrophically fail generation (BLEU-4 [≤] 0.0001); moreover, the domain-specific BioViL-T also fails classification (11.5% accuracy). From a data-engineering angle, the pipeline is productionizable with lineage, feature registries, and continuous integration to guard against silent regressions when updating models or data; from a data-science angle, the benchmark provides baselines and analyses that foreground feature alignment and architectural suitability as first-order concerns, inviting ablations on multimodal objectives, retrieval-augmented encoders, and uncertainty-aware decoding. Overall, RadMultiBench highlights that state-of-the-art status in general V-L domains does not translate automatically to high-stakes clinical tasks, and it furnishes the tooling and evidence base needed to develop robust, clinically viable multimodal systems.

papers.title: Inferring gene regulatory networks from single-cell perturbation data by optimizing causal reach of latent mediator dynamics
papers.abstract: Resolving the causal structure of gene regulatory networks is central to understanding cellular regulation. Pooled CRISPR screens with single-cell RNA readouts measure the transcriptional consequences of many interventions in parallel, providing a powerful resource for causal discovery. Combinatorial designs that perturb multiple regulators per cell increase throughput and can reveal responses that single-gene perturbations do not. However, inferring causal gene networks from these experiments remains challenging because gene regulatory interactions are nonlinear, dynamic, and often involve feedback. Thus, attributing the combined effect of several perturbations to individual regulators remains difficult. Additionally, transcriptional regulation is ultimately carried out by proteins, while single-cell perturbation datasets generally measure only RNA levels. Existing methods often simplify regulatory dynamics or rely on assumptions that conflict with gene regulation, such as acyclicity. Moreover, current evaluation practices usually rely on expression prediction error, which is readily computable in real datasets, but does not necessarily reflect graph quality. A complementary metric is needed to assess inferred regulatory connections using observed perturbation responses in real data. To address these challenges, we present CausalODE, a differentiable framework for learning causal graphs from single-cell perturbation data. Our approach incorporates three central insights to improve upon previous methods. First, genes that are differentially expressed when a gene is perturbed should be downstream of the target gene in the regulatory network; we quantify this property with a metric we term causal reach. Second, causal interactions involve transient cellular responses in RNA transcription, splicing, and degradation. Third, gene regulatory interactions are mediated by proteins, whose levels are not directly measured in single-cell RNA-seq experiments. Building on these insights, CausalODE learns a graph that optimizes the causal reach metric, captures transient cellular responses to perturbation, and explicitly models the latent dynamics of protein levels. Together, these components allow nonlinear responses, feedback loops, and time-lagged regulation. Across simulated Perturb-seq datasets with different sparsities and graph structures, CausalODE improves AUPRC and precision among top-ranked edges compared with baselines and competing methods, while achieving competitive AUROC. We introduce a metric to evaluate the causal reach of inferred graphs on real data by measuring how well the graphs explain differentially expressed genes in single-cell perturbation experiments. Using this metric, CausalODE outperforms the strongest competing method or baseline by approximately 60% on the CaRPool-seq knockdown dataset and 80% on the Norman et al. activation dataset. Its top-ranked edges generally show greater enrichment for high-confidence evidence from cell-type-matched ChIP-seq, CollecTRI, and regulatory STRING than those of other methods. The inferred graphs also distinguish non-additive from approximately additive genetic interactions in held-out perturbation pairs. Finally, ablation analyses show that optimizing causal reach improves performance on held-out perturbations, and the learned latent regulator activities track simulated protein dynamics, with median temporal correlations ranging from 0.79 to 0.99.

papers.title: Rapid, accurate, and memory-frugal sub-gene-level quantification of probe-based, multiplexed single-cell data
papers.abstract: Probe-based, multiplexed single-cell assays enable accurate transcriptome profiling while processing multiple samples in parallel. Their predefined probe sequences and additional sample barcodes introduce computational requirements that differ from those of poly(A)-based assays, for which many existing single-cell quantification tools were developed. We extend simpleaf to enable efficient demultiplexing and quantification of probe-based single-cell libraries. A new, cache-friendly dictionary specializes lookup to small probe references, while a shared thread budget balances parallel decompression and mapping. We extend RAD and downstream tools with reusable sample-scoped correction plans and external-memory collation of hierarchically barcoded data, retaining probe identities through quantification to enable rapid mapping and quantification with a small working memory budget. Across five 10x Genomics Flex datasets comprising 44 samples, simpleaf had the shortest runtime and lowest peak memory use of the three tools on every library, while producing gene-expression estimates, cell clusters, and marker genes concordant with cyto and Cell Ranger. Compared with cyto, simpleaf was on average 2 times faster and used approximately one-thirteenth as much memory. simpleaf also exports probe-level quantification results, allowing a range of analyses at sub-gene resolution. Here, we show that individual probe counts reveal expression changes obscured by gene-level aggregation, identify the transcript groups contributing to gene-level changes, and provide insight into splicing dynamics across cell types. These results demonstrate the computational and biological value of retaining probe-level information in multiplexed singlecell analysis.

papers.title: Organotchi: an open-source tool for the automated segmentation, morphological characterization, and longitudinal tracking of organoids
papers.abstract: Neural organoids are three-dimensional stem cell-derived models widely used to study brain development and model disease. Brightfield imaging offers a non-invasive readout of their growth and morphology, and recent advances have made automated organoid segmentation from such images increasingly attainable. Yet existing tools largely leave morphological characterization, quality assessment, and comparisons between conditions to manual or ad hoc analysis. Here we present Organotchi, an open-source tool that integrates automated segmentation with longitudinal morphological analysis of neural organoids. Organotchi quantifies ten morphological features, including area, perimeter, and eccentricity, and tracks cystic structures over time, reports variability within and between batches, and flags outlier organoids and segmentation failures, supporting objective organoid characterization and enhancing downstream analysis. As a proof of concept, we apply Organotchi to disease modelling, pharmacological perturbation, and protocol optimization in neural organoids. One use case assesses drug response in breast cancer spheroids, demonstrating its use beyond its development domain.

papers.title: TailEnrich enables discovery of dysregulated genes through disease sample enrichment testing
papers.abstract: Identifying differentially expressed genes is fundamental to elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying complex diseases. However, in complex disorders such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), the genes exhibiting dysregulated expression may vary among patient subsets, reflecting the heterogeneity of the underlying pathological processes. Consequently, pathogenic genes are profoundly dysregulated in only a subset of patients. Conventional differential expression tools, such as DESeq2 and edgeR, are primarily designed to detect population-level expression shifts and may have limited power to identify subgroup-specific dysregulation. To overcome this limitation, we developed TailEnrich, a novel computational method that discovers dysregulated genes within patient subsets. TailEnrich independently tests the extreme left (downregulated) or right (upregulated) tails of a gene's expression distribution for disease sample enrichment. We quantify this enrichment using a new metric, i.e. the PE (Percentage of Enriched disease samples) score. On simulated datasets, TailEnrich demonstrates markedly improved accuracy over DESeq2 and edgeR in identifying dysregulated genes specific to patient subsets. Applied to AD gene expression data, TailEnrich uncovers a distinct, biologically relevant set of genes within key pathological pathways that are missed by mean shift-based approaches. TailEnrich provides a novel method for identifying dysregulated genes, and readily extends to other omics data including genomic variants and proteomics to uncover pathogenic genes in complex diseases.

papers.title: Agentic AI enables cell segmentation-free cell-type inference and cell-type-guided cell segmentation in spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Cell-type identification in spatial transcriptomics often relies on cell segmentation, which can introduce inaccuracies in cell boundaries and transcript assignment. Segmentation-free or cell-free methods have been developed to completely avoid cell segmentation, but inaccurate cell typing hinder accurate downstream analysis. Here, we introduce SSAF-T, a segmentation-free agentic framework that identifies cell types directly from spatial gene expression without predefined reference datasets. For the reference-free cell typing, SSAF-T incorporates CeLLMan, which employs expert-level agents for each organ to annotate cell types using a literature-grounded knowledge graph. We benchmark SSAF-T on both array-based and imaging-based spatial transcriptomics datasets in terms of accuracy, reproducibility, and scalability. We further show that SSAF-T provides an accurate cell segmentation based on the segmentation-free mapping, which ensure compatibility to existing downstream analysis ecosystem, and eventually enable quantitative analysis at single-cell level.

papers.title: Residual barcode-like sequences and barcode-associated artifacts after Dorado and Barbell preprocessing of metagenomic reads
papers.abstract: Background Residual barcode-like sequences after preprocessing are a quality-control concern in multiplexed Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) sequencing data, particularly in low-biomass, host-dominated samples such as blood. Using blood datasets spiked with a microbial mock community and prepared with the Native Barcoding Kit 96 V14 (SQK-NBD114.96), we compared Dorado 1.1.1, Dorado 2.0.0, and Barbell 0.3.2. Results Dorado demultiplexing reduced barcode-positive reads to approximately 2% of reads, with internal barcode-like matches in 0.17-0.19% of reads. Barbell 0.3.2 applied to untrimmed Dorado basecalls yielded an approximately 50-fold lower detector-defined internal-match rate (0.0035-0.0037%) while retaining 91.2-91.8% of input reads. In the NCBI core_nt release of 12 September 2026, the focused screen identified complete, ungapped 24 nt identity for 64 of the 96 barcodes (66.7%), comprising 505 distinct barcode-accession pairs across 482 accessions and 195 exported TaxID groups of mixed taxonomic ranks. Records annotated as rRNA genes, chromosomes/genomes, and plasmids accounted for 35.6%, 23.2%, and 22.4% of the pairs, respectively. The barcode was located within its native ligation flanks in 224 pairs (44.4%), including 170 (33.7%) with the complete Dorado barcode search window and 3 (0.6%) with the full adapter construct. Conclusion Barbell combined 91-92% read retention with lower detected internal barcode signals. After demultiplexing, barcode-like sequences remained in sample data. Moreover, kit barcode sequences, often within their native ligation flanks, were detected in reference records. Both findings call for careful preprocessing, reference inspection, and downstream validation. Further research should determine whether barcode-associated artifacts in reads and reference records affect taxonomic classification in clinical metagenomic workflows.

papers.title: Predicting Transcriptional Responses to Unseen Compounds through Context Modeling and Multi-View Transfer
papers.abstract: Predicting drug-induced transcriptional responses could support in silico screening of new compounds, yet existing models barely use the compound: on a drug-blind L1000 benchmark, removing the drug input from seven published models changes accuracy by at most 0.012 Pearson correlation. They capture shared cellular and experimental variation while overlooking the compound-specific signals that distinguish drug effects. We present UnDetect, a framework that separates contextual variation from compound effects to predict responses to transcriptionally unprofiled compounds. UnDetect integrates chemical structure, annotated targets, mechanisms of action and Cell Painting morphology into a normalized multi-view kernel that accommodates incomplete compound information, and transfers residual responses within and across profiled cell lines, so that pharmacological and phenotypic relationships inform predictions beyond chemical similarity. On a drug-blind benchmark, where the paired control reveals the assay plate, UnDetect is the only model to beat a network that ignores the compound, in every fold; on a within-plate score that is zero for any compound-blind prediction, it reaches 0.117 against 0.092 for the strongest published model. On DeepCE's benchmark it reaches 0.602 Pearson correlation against the reported 0.491. Transfer across cell lines improves 28 of 28 LINCS L1000 and, at the two higher doses, 47 and 49 of 50 Tahoe-100M cell-line evaluations. These results show that separating context from compound effects and integrating complementary compound information improves transcriptional prediction and extends the utility of perturbation atlases for virtual screening.

papers.title: Growing a Root from Its Genome : Emergent Tissue Layers and Zones in a GPU-Native Simulation of the Arabidopsis Root Tip
papers.abstract: Models of the Arabidopsis root tip usually take its cell identities as given. Here we grow a root tip from a single genome. In a two-dimensional median section, every cell reads the same network of 62 genes (26 core genes from an earlier, unpublished model of callus and 36 added for the root) and starts with the same expression; the only spatial cues are the polarity of auxin transport, auxin from the shoot and the free surface. Identities and zones are never given to the simulation; they are read from gene expression. Cells are polygons of a shared mesh, relaxed towards mechanical equilibrium under turgor at every step. In 48 simulated hours, a tip-shaped template grows into a root of 3 000-4 500 cells with epidermis, cortex, endodermis, pericycle and stele in order along most of its length, SHORT-ROOT and SCARECROW in the endodermis, an auxin maximum, a quiescent centre and a cap at its tip, and meristem, elongation and mature zones. A WOX5 gate built from published interactions and one hypothesis keeps a quiescent centre to 48 h in 17 of 20 simulated roots that were not used for tuning (85%; Wilson 95% interval 64-95%; criteria fixed before the run), against 9 of 20 roots used for tuning, before the gate. The niche is not maintained beyond 48 h: grown on to 73 h, only 6 of these 20 roots still have a quiescent centre (30%; 15-52%). All pre-registered criteria hold in only 1 of 20 roots, because the quiescent centre is too wide at 0 h; without that count, 12 of 20. The meristem is too long, and cortical cells made after the start of growth elongate only three- to four-fold instead of eightto thirty-fold, a limit set in large part by the numerical growth scheme. Mutants are a major weakness: several look like their published phenotype, but an exploratory re-run of a mutant benchmark fixed in advance for our first model passes one of nine predictions. Nor does the root regenerate: cut near its tip, it re-forms an auxin maximum and a columella but no quiescent centre. On a first, simpler model and without any polarity cue, a mass of identical cells still sorts into concentric layers and, when PIN carriers follow the auxin flux, concentrates auxin into a few foci, but forms no stem-cell niche: the genome lacks a lateral inhibition between foci. We state the limitations and the next stages.

papers.title: DisCell: Separating Spillover from Niche Response in Spatial Transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics at single-cell resolution measures every cell in its place in the tissue, but diffusion and segmentation errors also add transcripts of neighboring cells to a cell's counts. This spillover makes a cell resemble its neighbors, and a response to the niche makes cells in the same niche resemble each other. Both tie a cell's expression to its surroundings. The count data alone cannot tell the two apart. Findings from single-cell transcriptomes, such as a gene program that is higher in one niche than in another or signaling genes that change depending on the neighborhood, may therefore be artifacts of spillover. Current models describe a cell by its intrinsic state together with either its niche response or spillover, but none models all three. We present DisCell, the first method that models all three components jointly and measures how robust each finding is to spillover. DisCell is a generative model that describes single-cell gene expression profiles in terms of two latent variables, an intrinsic state and a response to the niche, and adds spillover from its neighbors as a separate term. DisCell fits the model at increasing levels of spillover and recomputes each finding on the spillover-free expression to see how much spillover it withstands. DisCell also estimates the most spillover a section can contain, and a finding that holds even at that amount is not explained by spillover. In simulated tissue, DisCell recovers each cell's intrinsic state and response and tells findings created by spillover apart from genuine responses. On five sections of ovarian and lung tissue, the intrinsic state keeps more of each cell's own properties, measured by its cell-cycle phase, than any competing method that holds as little of its neighborhood. Within each cell type, the model partitions the variation of each gene into intrinsic state, niche response and spillover. Using DisCell, we rank findings about niches by their robustness to spillover and confirm that a previously reported finding withstands spillover, that esophageal cancer cells in niches infiltrated by immune or stromal cells express more of an epithelial-mesenchymal transition program. DisCell also predicts what the gene expression of a cell type would be in another niche, with its spillover part separated, at lower error on most tasks than the competing method built for this purpose. Training the model takes under ten minutes on one consumer GPU for sections of up to 400,000 cells.
